title: New York Times Co. v. Microsoft & OpenAI — opinion largely denying motions to dismiss
pub: S.D.N.Y., Opinion & Order on Motions to Dismiss
author: Sidney H. Stein

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion adjudicates pleading sufficiency in copyright, DMCA and trademark disputes; it does not assess legal-work redesign, selective deployment, user expertise, verification or organisational value. Its discussion of LLM behaviour largely recounts allegations assumed true for dismissal purposes, so it cannot establish a position on the cluster’s proposition.
qs: BACKGROUND      The following facts are taken from the plaintiffs’ complaints and assumed to be true for the purpose of evaluating defendants’ motions to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6).

kp.k: Rulings concern plausible allegations, not established AI infringement
kp.d: Judge Sidney H. Stein evaluates selected claims in the Times, Daily News and CIR actions under pleading standards, assuming well-pleaded facts true. The opinion addresses copyright, copyright-management information and trademark risks arising from generative AI, rather than changes to legal staffing or service delivery. Survival of claims does not establish defendants’ liability.
qs: The following facts are taken from the plaintiffs’ complaints and assumed to be true for the purpose of evaluating defendants’ motions to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6).

kp.k: Publishers challenge both training copies and generated outputs
kp.d: The complaints distinguish collecting and copying journalism for model training from outputs allegedly reproducing memorized material. They also allege that search-connected outputs substitute for visits to publishers’ websites. These are plaintiffs’ descriptions of the systems and economic harms, not independently established technical or market findings.
qs: According to the complaints, defendants’ LLMs implicate plaintiffs’ works at two stages: (1) the training stage, where defendants use a corpus of text—including plaintiffs’ works—to train their LLMs, and (2) the “output” stage, where defendants’ LLMs generate outputs in response to user prompts that, according to the complaints, “regurgitate” plaintiffs’ works.

According to plaintiffs, these outputs generate “extensive paraphrases and direct quotes” of plaintiffs’ works, without referring users to plaintiffs’ websites in the same manner as do regular internet search engines, thereby obviating the need for users to visit plaintiffs’ websites.

kp.k: Discovery rule preserves older training-related infringement claims
kp.d: The court rejects OpenAI’s limitations defense at this stage for Times and Daily News claims concerning conduct more than three years before filing. Public reporting about internet-scale training did not establish notice of specific copying before December 27, 2020 and April 30, 2021 respectively. The court leaves open whether discovery will establish earlier knowledge and rejects heightened diligence based merely on publisher sophistication.
qs: OpenAI has not met its burden of establishing that The Times and the Daily News plaintiffs discovered, or with due diligence should have discovered, the alleged infringement before December 27, 2020 and April 30, 2021 respectively.
Discovery may reveal facts supporting OpenAI’s contention that The Times and the Daily News plaintiffs discovered the alleged infringement before December 27, 2020 and April 30, 2021 respectively.

kp.k: End-user infringement supports alternative contributory liability claims
kp.d: All three plaintiffs plausibly plead contributory infringement as an alternative if end users, rather than defendants, are directly liable for generated outputs. Complaint examples and alleged public reports support an inference of third-party infringement. Applying Second Circuit law rather than defendants’ proposed Ninth Circuit standard, the court finds actual or constructive knowledge adequately alleged; defendants did not challenge material contribution.
qs: Plaintiffs bring those claims in the alternative to their direct infringement claims to the extent third-party end users—not defendants—are found liable for direct infringement for generating infringing outputs using defendants’ LLMs.
The Court finds that plaintiffs have plausibly alleged the existence of third-party end-user infringement and that defendants knew or had reason to know of that infringement.
Defendants do not challenge the “material contribution” component of plaintiffs’ contributory copyright infringement claim.

kp.k: Lawful uses do not foreclose contributory claims here
kp.d: The court rejects substantial noninfringing uses as a basis for dismissal at the pleading stage. It distinguishes the asserted material-contribution theory from inducement and emphasizes defendants’ continuing interactions with users and allegations that their products incorporate appropriated works. It analogizes supplying both protected material and an infringement mechanism to supplying an unauthorized adaptation, rather than merely selling copying equipment.
qs: Sony and Grokster do not foreclose plaintiffs’ contributory copyright infringement claims at this stage for at least three reasons.
Here, however, an “ongoing relationship” exists between defendants and end users, via defendants’ LLM outputs that respond to end users’ prompts.
Second, the VTR was not a product that itself was built on purportedly appropriated works, as are defendants’ products here.

kp.k: Alleged CMI removal establishes standing through copyright-related harms
kp.d: The court finds Article III and statutory standing for the DMCA claims, distinct from whether those claims are adequately pleaded on their merits. Traditional copyright injury supplies a historical analogue for harm from removing copyright management information. Alleged concealment and facilitation of infringement, website diversion and lost subscription or licensing revenue establish sufficiently concrete and traceable injury.
qs: Here, traditional copyright law provides that “close historical or common-law analogue” and supports plaintiffs’ claims of harm.
Here, plaintiffs allege that defendants’ removal of CMI from plaintiffs’ works conceals and facilitates copyright infringement, which deprives plaintiffs of licensing and subscription revenue.
Assuming without deciding that section 1203(a) requires allegations of injury beyond a mere statutory violation, plaintiffs have satisfied this requirement.

kp.k: Specific extraction allegations sustain some CMI-removal claims
kp.d: Daily News and CIR plausibly allege intentional removal under section 1202(b)(1) through OpenAI’s use of Dragnet and Newspaper extraction tools. They also adequately allege knowledge that removal could conceal OpenAI’s own infringement or facilitate end-user infringement. The Times’ inference from CMI-less output excerpts is insufficient without specific training-process allegations. All removal claims against Microsoft fail for lack of defendant-specific facts. These dismissals are without prejudice.
qs: The Daily News and CIR complaints, however, plausibly allege CMI removal during the LLM training process.
it is entirely plausible that CMI remained on the articles included in the training datasets but simply did not appear in the outputs.
plaintiffs have plausibly alleged both that OpenAI’s removal of CMI conceals its own infringement, and that that removal enables and facilitates third-party infringement.

None of the allegations concerning Microsoft—including Microsoft’s partnership with OpenAI to develop Copilot and Browse with Bing, and its provision of the cloud computing system which OpenAI uses to train its models—relate to any alleged removal by Microsoft of CMI from plaintiffs’ works.

kp.k: Output excerpts fail DMCA distribution claims
kp.d: The court dismisses Times and Daily News section 1202(b)(3) claims without prejudice because the pleaded outputs reproduce excerpts rather than substantially or entirely reproducing the underlying works. It expressly leaves unresolved whether LLM outputs constitute distributions rather than public displays. This DMCA ruling does not determine whether the excerpts infringe copyright under other theories.
qs: Assuming without deciding that the LLM regurgitations do constitute “distributions,” plaintiffs have another hurdle to clear: they must show that those regurgitations constitute “works” or “copies of works.”

Accordingly, because the outputs are merely excerpts of plaintiffs’ works and not “copies” of those works for purposes of section 1202(b)(3), The Times and the Daily News plaintiffs have failed to establish that defendants “distributed” “copies” of their works in violation of section 1202(b)(3), and their section 1202(b)(3) claims against defendants are dismissed.

kp.k: Commercial partnership does not establish distribution between defendants
kp.d: CIR’s alternative DMCA theory—that Microsoft and OpenAI distributed CMI-less copies to one another—also fails without prejudice. Investment, computing infrastructure and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s statement about possessing data do not supply facts establishing transfers of CIR articles. The court reads the CEO’s remark in its surrounding discussion of Microsoft’s independent ability to continue AI development.
qs: CIR’s allegations about the general business relationship between OpenAI and Microsoft fail to indicate that OpenAI “distributed” “copies” of CIR’s articles to Microsoft.

Nowhere in the complaint’s lengthy discussion of OpenAI’s process of training its models on works scraped from the internet does CIR allege when, why, or how OpenAI would have “distributed” copies of those works to Microsoft.

kp.k: Copyright preemption defeats news and recommendation misappropriation claims
kp.d: The court dismisses common-law unfair-competition claims with prejudice. The narrow hot-news exception requires additional elements, including time sensitivity and free-riding. Source-identifying prompts and outputs undermine non-attribution allegations; other examples lack allegations of immediate appropriation when profit would be earned. Wirecutter allegations likewise fail because outputs attribute recommendations and the alleged affiliate-link losses are not time-specific.
qs: While the outputs listed in plaintiffs’ complaints may well raise copyright concerns, they do not suffer from non-attribution, which is central to the “free riding” element of a “hot news” misappropriation claim.

Instead, the complaint alleges that The Times suffers harm from the removal of Wirecutter’s affiliate links—from which The Times receives a commission—in defendants’ LLM outputs, a harm that is not time-specific.

Accordingly, the common law unfair competition by misappropriation claims included in plaintiffs’ complaints are preempted by section 301 of the Copyright Act, and defendants’ motions to dismiss those claims are granted.

kp.k: False attribution creates a pleaded trademark dilution dispute
kp.d: Certain Daily News plaintiffs allege tarnishment through inaccurate AI writing attributed to their publications. OpenAI challenges whether the marks are famous; the court finds sufficiently detailed allegations of longstanding publication, national circulation, consumer reach and recognition. This is a ruling on the adequacy of fame allegations, not a determination that dilution occurred.
qs: They allege that defendants have used the Diluted Trademarks, without authorization, “on lower-quality and inaccurate writing,” thereby “dilut[ing] the quality of the Diluted Trademarks by tarnishment, in violation of [section] 1125(c).”
The Court therefore denies OpenAI’s motion to dismiss the federal trademark dilution claim in the Daily News action.

kp.k: Interstate AI activity does not invalidate state dilution protection
kp.d: The court rejects Microsoft’s dormant Commerce Clause challenge to New York’s dilution statute. Practical effects outside New York do not alone invalidate a nondiscriminatory law. Microsoft showed neither discrimination against out-of-state commerce nor incidental burdens clearly exceeding local benefits, leaving the Daily News state-law dilution claim standing.
qs: The New York dilution statute may “have a considerable influence on commerce outside [New York’s] borders,” id. at 375, but Microsoft has not contended much less shown that section 360-l discriminates against out-of-state commerce.

Accordingly, Microsoft’s motion to dismiss the trademark dilution plaintiffs’ state dilution claim is denied, because Microsoft has not shown that N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law § 360-l discriminates against out of state commerce or that its incidental burdens on interstate commerce are in clear excess of its local benefits.

kp.k: Specific factual summaries lack substantial similarity to protected expression
kp.d: The court dismisses with prejudice CIR’s direct-infringement theory concerning the abridgments in Exhibit 11. Those outputs summarize facts, generally through bullet points or short paragraphs, using different arrangement, phrasing, style and sentence structure. The holding concerns these particular examples and distinguishes unprotected facts from protected expression; it does not dispose of all direct-infringement allegations.
qs: The alleged abridgments are detailed summaries, usually in bullet point form, of the facts contained in CIR’s articles.
Those summaries—which differ in style, tone, length, and sentence structure from CIR’s articles—are not “substantially similar” to CIR’s copyrighted works.
The Court therefore grants OpenAI’s motion to dismiss CIR’s claim of direct infringement under 17 U.S.C. § 501 insofar as it relates to the “abridgments” contained in Exhibit 11.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: This cross-domain opinion addresses AI’s alleged effects on journalism and the legal boundaries of training, reproducing, summarizing, and falsely attributing news content—not changes to legal-service delivery.
pts.d: Judge Sidney H. Stein recounts the publishers’ allegations that defendants use their journalism to train LLMs, which can reproduce article excerpts and supply internet-derived answers that substitute for visiting publishers’ websites. Publishers allege resulting losses of subscription, advertising, licensing, and affiliate revenue, alongside reputational harm from falsely attributed output. These are allegations evaluated at the pleading stage, not established market effects. Stein holds that contributory copyright infringement is plausibly alleged and allows specified CMI-removal and trademark-dilution claims to proceed. Conversely, he concludes that the particular CIR summaries are not substantially similar to protected expression, that the pleaded excerpt outputs do not constitute copies for the DMCA distribution claims, and that the unfair-competition claims are preempted. The opinion does not determine generally whether AI training is lawful or forecast the future of journalism.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is complaints, attached output examples, allegations about data-extraction methods, and legal precedent—not an empirical study of AI’s market effects.
pts.d: Stein relies on examples in the Times, Daily News, and CIR complaints to assess whether end-user infringement is plausible. Allegations concerning Dragnet and Newspaper content extractors support the Daily News and CIR claims that OpenAI intentionally removed copyright management information during dataset preparation; the Times’s inference from missing CMI in outputs alone is insufficient. His conclusion about CIR’s abridgments rests on comparison of the exhibited summaries with the underlying articles. The legal analysis applies copyright, DMCA, trademark, standing, and preemption authorities. No measured revenue losses, representative output-error rates, or causal market estimates are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The April 4, 2025 opinion evaluates alleged past and continuing conduct under pleading-stage standards, without a future forecast.
pts.d: The actions were filed in December 2023, April 2024, and June 2024. Disputed training activity includes conduct in 2019 and 2020; output allegations concern products released subsequently, including ChatGPT in November 2022 and Browse with Bing in May 2023. Refusing to dismiss older infringement claims does not finally resolve timeliness: discovery could establish earlier actual or constructive knowledge. Contributory infringement is pleaded alternatively if end users, rather than defendants, are found directly liable. Surviving claims establish plausibility, not liability. The ruling on summaries is confined to the abridgments in CIR’s Exhibit 11, rather than all AI-generated summaries. DMCA dismissals are without prejudice; unfair-competition and specified abridgment dismissals are with prejudice.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected parties are news publishers, AI developers and operators, and end users consuming or eliciting journalism through AI systems.
pts.d: The publishers comprise the Times and Wirecutter, eight local newspapers, and CIR’s nonprofit investigative brands. Their alleged exposure includes audience diversion, reduced revenues supporting reporting, loss of affiliate commissions, and reputational injury from falsely attributed content. Microsoft and OpenAI face continuing litigation over selected copyright, CMI-removal, and dilution theories, while other claims are dismissed. End users allegedly obtain publishers’ material without visiting or subscribing to their sites and may themselves infringe copyright by eliciting protected output. The opinion does not identify effects on law-firm staffing, legal fees, or access to justice.
